thread.title: Mayor Sheffield orders all city commercial property sale proceeds to affordable housing fund
thread.title_full: Mayor Sheffield orders all city commercial property sale proceeds to affordable housing fund

author: G. G. Haynes
title: Mayor Sheffield orders all city commercial property sale proceeds to affordable housing fund
text:
Mayor Mary Sheffield announced on Mar. 25 that all proceeds from the sale of city-owned commercial properties in Detroit will be directed to the Affordable Housing Development and Preservation Trust Fund, more than doubling the current contribution. The new Executive Order increases the allocation from 40% to 100%, raising expected annual contributions from just under $2 million to about $4 million.
The move is intended to boost efforts to build and preserve affordable housing across Detroit, supporting residents at risk of displacement due to rising costs. The Trust Fund provides gap financing, low-interest loans, and grants for developers focused on keeping units affordable.
Sheffield said, “The Affordable Housing Trust Fund has been a great tool that has helped several important projects get past the planning stage and eventually built to provide deeply affordable and permanent supportive housing for our most vulnerable residents.” She added, “Directing 100% of commercial property sale proceeds to the Trust Fund is one of the many ways my administration is going to increase our capacity to build more affordable housing.”
Recent projects supported by the fund include LaJoya Gardens in Southwest Detroit with 42 new units for households earning between 30% and 80% of Area Median Income (AMI), The Residences at St. Matthews which repurposed a former school into permanent supportive housing for homeless individuals as well as additional affordable units, and The Hive near Eastern Market offering new construction with rents based on incomes at or below 60% AMI. LaJoya Gardens received a $1.1 million investment from the fund; rents there start at $540 per month.
Under current ordinance rules spearheaded by Sheffield in her time as council member, at least 70% of trust expenditures over any three-year period must support those making no more than 30% AMI; remaining funds go toward those earning up to half of AMI. Units funded through this mechanism are required to remain affordable for at least thirty years—with priority given where affordability can be maintained indefinitely.
“To have a healthy city that is affordable to people of all income levels, affordability must be sustainable, and long-term rent commitments in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund help with that sustainability,” said Sheffield.
The Executive Order will take effect July 1, coinciding with Detroit’s new fiscal year.
